source.title: [Replication] Conjecture's Sparse Coding in Small Transformers

record.file_problem: Full post text is present; figure contents are not included, but several outcomes are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoder feature recovery to activations from a custom-trained small transformer, a new setting relative to toy-model experiments, and reports results on the recovered features.
record.gate_note: The post reports dictionary-size comparisons, feature similarity, training progress, neuron-basis diversity, and qualitative examples. Hyperparameter values and the cited random-vector simulation are not counted as separate results; the simulation is attributed to Robert Huben. The diagonal-line artifact is noted as a methodological correction, not a result about the claim.
record.test_reason: The post applies sparse autoencoders to MLP activations of a custom small transformer. It reports whether many more features than dimensions can be recovered (V4) and whether they recur across dictionary sizes (V5). This is a new setting with results on both versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors replicate Sharkey et al.'s core results: many more features than dimensions are recovered, MCS across dictionary sizes is bimodal, and a consistent feature set recurs. Convergence for larger dictionaries is unresolved; MMCS plateaus and improves only slowly with training. Features are not sparse in the neuron basis. Max-activating examples look interpretable, but the authors explicitly say no systematic comparison has been done.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparse autoencoders and cross-dictionary feature comparison on activations from a custom-trained small transformer rather than toy-generated data; it evaluates a transformer layer and reports neuron-basis diversity as well.
record.method_sensitivity: The diagonal patterns in the earlier hyperparameter sweeps were attributed to dividing the l1-loss term by dictionary size. Removing that division allowed use of a consistent l1 coefficient across dictionary sizes. Dictionary size and additional autoencoder training are associated with changes in alignment results.

fits_no_version.finding: Learned features, including the recurrent ones, are not sparse in the neuron basis. The authors present this as contrary to what some models, including Toy Models of Superposition, predict.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in real models would be sparse in the MLP neuron basis, as some toy-model accounts of how MLPs use the nonlinearity predict.

record.problems: Only one custom-trained small transformer and layer 2 are reported. Numerical MMCS values and uncertainty estimates are absent from the text. Convergence with further training is unresolved. Interpretability is assessed qualitatively from selected maximum activations, not systematically. The authors note two outlier exceptions in the neuron-basis sparsity result.

untested.parts: Not tested: storage as nearly orthogonal directions in a toy model, a sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry.
Not tested: capacity competition, or whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
Not tested: alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Only one small model and one layer are tested. There is no larger LLM, and no quantitative interpretability comparison with the neuron basis, PCA or ICA.
Not tested: completeness of the dictionary, or canonicity beyond cross-size cosine matching.
Not tested: whether features are 1-D or multi-dimensional.

missing.what: Summary result: as dictionary size increases, MMCS rises rapidly at first, then plateaus. Also, the number of highly similar features grows with dictionary size, but more slowly than the number of unrelated features.
missing.locator: Summary bullets; Bi-modality of MCS scores section

record.verdict_notes: The record mislabels the activation space: SAEs were trained on the 128-dim layer-2 MLP activations, not the 32-dim residual stream. The reader's V5 'challenges' label for r4 is too strong, because many non-matching features are dead and the matching core grows with size; it is relabelled limits_scope. The diagonal-line artifact is a methodological fix, not a result. The random-vector MCS simulation is Huben's.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether the transformer itself stores sparse features as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, or test a sparsity-dependent transition or regular geometry.
Does not test whether neuron polysemanticity results from competition for limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Does not investigate alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Tests feature recovery and the distribution of learned feature vectors in one small transformer, but not a broad range of real models or a systematic comparison with the neuron basis.
Measures similarity of learned features across dictionary sizes, but does not establish that SAE features are complete or canonical units.
Does not test whether the underlying features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: small transformer (nanoGPT)
rows.size_stated: 6 layers, 32 dimensional residual stream, MLP widths of 128 and 4 attention heads with dimension 8
rows.operation_detail: Applied sparse autoencoders to layer 2 activations and compared learned dictionaries across dictionary sizes using MMCS-with-larger.
rows.measure: MMCS-with-larger similarity of features in smaller dictionaries to features in larger dictionaries
rows.value: High MMCS-with-larger scores for smaller dictionaries; the text says many more features than the activation-space dimension could be recovered.
rows.note: The text describes high similarity across dictionaries but does not give numerical MMCS values.
rows.check: Activations are the 128-dim layer-2 MLP activations (Figure 1 caption), not the 32-dim residual stream. Observed holds only for smaller dictionaries; the text says larger-dictionary results 'seem mixed'.

source_check.locator_found: Background; MMCS-with-larger Results, Figure 1; Bi-modality of MCS scores, Figure 2.

rows.subject: small transformer (nanoGPT)
rows.size_stated: 6 layers, 32 dimensional residual stream, MLP widths of 128 and 4 attention heads with dimension 8
rows.operation_detail: Measured the distribution of maximum cosine similarity scores between features learned by dictionaries of different sizes.
rows.measure: Distribution of maximum cosine similarity (MCS) scores
rows.value: The distribution is described as highly bimodal, with a high-similarity group and a peak around 0.25–0.4 that the post says is close to the distribution expected for random directions.
rows.note: The cited random-vector simulation is attributed to Robert Huben, not reported as an experiment by the post authors.
rows.check: Bimodality means a consistent core of features plus a random-like group, so stability across sizes is partial. This is about cross-dictionary stability, not V4 recovery. The random-vector reference comes from Huben's simulation.
